title: DRA: GatherPools completeness is order-dependent when ResourceSliceCount values disagree
author: thc1006
body:
### What happened?

`GatherPools` determines whether a pool generation is complete by comparing the number of retained slices with `slicesForPool[0].Spec.Pool.ResourceSliceCount`, so the declared count comes from the first retained slice for that pool generation. When two ResourceSlices in the same driver, pool, and generation disagree on `ResourceSliceCount`, the same set of objects can be classified differently under different input permutations. In my direct allocator reproduction, `slice-a` declares `resourceSliceCount: 1` and contains one device, while `slice-b` declares `resourceSliceCount: 2` and contains one device. With `[slice-a, slice-b]`, the generation is treated as incomplete and its devices are not offered; with `[slice-b, slice-a]`, it is treated as complete and is built. Only the input order changes.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pool-generation completeness should be invariant under permutations of the ResourceSlice input. ResourceSlices in the same `(driver, pool, generation)` describe one pool revision and should agree on the total `ResourceSliceCount`. When they do not, `GatherPools` should fail closed deterministically—for example, by treating the generation as invalid or otherwise unavailable for allocation—rather than accepting the contradictory revision in one ordering and rejecting it in another. Slice order may legitimately affect candidate preference, but it should not determine whether a revision is complete.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Construct two ResourceSlices in the same `(driver, pool, generation)`: `slice-a` with `resourceSliceCount: 1` and one device, and `slice-b` with `resourceSliceCount: 2` and one device. Invoke the structured allocator with a claim for one device, once with each ResourceSlice input order. `[slice-a, slice-b]` yields no allocation because the pool is considered incomplete, while `[slice-b, slice-a]` allocates. Two controls isolate the count disagreement from device capacity: consistent counts `{2, 2}` allocate in both orders, while consistent counts `{1, 1}` with two slices are incomplete in both orders. I reproduced the same order-dependent result in the stable, incubating, and experimental allocator variants.

### Anything else we need to know?

The slower completeness path does not remove the order dependence because it also compares the number of discovered slices against `slicesForPool[0].Spec.Pool.ResourceSliceCount`. The source already contains `Future TODO: detect inconsistent ResourceSliceCount, also in poolIsInvalid`; this report concerns the observable consequence of not yet performing that check, rather than merely requesting implementation of the existing TODO. Per-object API validation does not detect the condition because each slice's count can be individually valid while the set is cross-object inconsistent.

This is a library-level observation against `GatherPools`. I reproduced it by invoking the structured allocator directly and did not verify the input ordering of any specific production consumer, so whether a particular consumer encounters the order-dependent result in practice depends on the order in which it supplies ResourceSlices.

A possible fix requires no API change: during the initial scan, track the expected `ResourceSliceCount` for each `(driver, pool, generation)`, fail closed when another slice declares a different value, apply the same behavior in all three allocator variants, and add regression coverage for both permutations. Whether the disagreement should be represented as invalid, incomplete, or otherwise unavailable for allocation is a maintainer decision. I am happy to send a PR if that direction sounds right.

title: kubectl get: PrintObj errors are silently discarded in human-readable output loop
author: Bhupesh-081
body:
### What happened?

When running kubectl get pods -o yaml (or any human-readable/structured output that goes through the per-object printer loop), errors returned by printer.PrintObj are silently discarded. The loop in Run() that iterates over fetched objects calls printer.PrintObj(info.Object, w) without checking the error return value, so a broken pipe, a closed writer, or any other IO failure during output is invisible to the caller. the command exits 0 regardless.

Relevant code:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/main/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/get/get.go#L569

```go
for _, info := range infos {
    ...
    printer.PrintObj(info.Object, w) // error return ignored
}
```


This is notable because the surrounding function already has an error-aggregation mechanism in place for this exact purpose. ToPrinter errors a few lines earlier are collected into an allErrs[] error slice and returned via utilerrors.NewAggregate(allErrs) at the end of Run(). The plumbing exists; PrintObj's return value just isn't fed into it.

A second occurrence of the identical pattern exists at staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/apply/prune.go#L137 printer.PrintObj(obj, p.out) inside a loop, in a function that returns error, with the result likewise ignored.



### What did you expect to happen?

Any error from printer.PrintObj in the loop should be captured, added to allErrs, and ultimately returned via the existing utilerrors.NewAggregate(allErrs) call, causing the command to exit non-zero consistent with how the ToPrinter error path in the same function already behaves:


```go
if err := printer.PrintObj(info.Object, w); err != nil {
    if !errs.Has(err.Error()) {
        errs.Insert(err.Error())
        allErrs = append(allErrs, err)
    }
}
```


### How can we reproduce it?

The easiest way to trigger this in a real cluster is to pipe the output to a program that exits early (causing a broken pipe):

```console
$ kubectl get pods -A | head -1
```


On Linux this triggers a broken-pipe write error at the OS level, but kubectl will still exit 0 because the error from PrintObj is swallowed.

A unit test can inject a writer that returns an error to confirm the bug programmatically.

### Anything else we need to know?

The fix is small: wrap the PrintObj call in the loop with the same error-collection pattern already used for ToPrinter errors a few lines above it in the same function. The same bug class exists in apply/prune.go:137 and should ideally be fixed alongside this, or filed as a linked follow-up.
Existing tests for get.go's output path cover the happy path only; none inject a failing writer, so this isn't caught by the current suite. A test covering printer-error propagation should be added with the fix.

title: kubectl patch: 'map does not contain declared merge key' error lacks actionable context
author: eilaytal
body:
## What happened

When using `kubectl patch` with a strategic merge patch on a list field without providing the required merge key, users see the following error:

```
Error from server: map: map[hostPath:map[path:/var/lib/kubelet/pods]] does not contain declared merge key: name
```

## What I expected

The error should explain:
1. **Which field** requires the merge key
2. **What** a merge key is and why it is required
3. **How to fix it** — i.e. include the merge key field in each list item
4. A short example of the correct format

## Reproduction

```bash
# Attempt to patch a container list without providing the "name" merge key
kubectl patch pod mypod --type=strategic -p '{"spec":{"containers":[{"image":"nginx:1.25"}]}}'
```

Expected: helpful error explaining that each list item needs `"name": "<container-name>"`
Actual: `map: map[...] does not contain declared merge key: name`

## Root cause

The error originates from `staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/mergepatch/errors.go` line 36:

```go
func ErrNoMergeKey(m map[string]interface{}, k string) error {
    return fmt.Errorf("map: %v does not contain declared merge key: %s", m, k)
}
```

The message prints the full map contents (potentially verbose) but provides no guidance on what the user needs to do to fix the patch.

## Suggested improvement

Something along the lines of:

```
Error: strategic merge patch requires merge key "name" in each list item.
When patching list/array fields, each item must include the merge key field so Kubernetes knows which item to update.
Example: {"spec": {"containers": [{"name": "my-container", "image": "nginx:1.25"}]}}
```

## Environment

- Kubernetes version: any (error message unchanged across recent versions)
- Component: `kubectl patch` / `apimachinery` strategic merge patch

/area kubectl
/kind documentation

title: DRA: ExtendedResourceCache serves stale mappings and can drop the winner across DeviceClass updates and collisions
author: thc1006
body:
The extended resource cache (`staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/deviceclass/extendedresourcecache/extendedresourcecache.go`, behind `DRAExtendedResource`) loses information it needs to keep `resourceName2class` correct across DeviceClass updates and explicit-name collisions. `updateResourceName2class` treats the class currently cached under an explicit name as a collision peer and arbitrates by creation timestamp and name, but that same path also runs when a class updates itself, and the removal paths delete by key without checking which class owns the entry.

Cases I traced on master:

1. A same-class update serves a stale object. On `OnUpdate` for a class that keeps its `ExtendedResourceName`, `updateResourceName2class` finds the cached (old) object under that name, sees an equal timestamp and equal name, and returns before replacing the pointer or re-adding the default mapping. `resourceName2class` keeps pointing at the old object while `class2ResourceName` is updated, so `GetDeviceClass(name)` returns the pre-update DeviceClass (stale selectors/config) until some unrelated event rewrites it.

2. A collision loser never gets its own implicit mapping. When the new class loses the explicit-name arbitration, the early `return` also skips the "Always add the default mapping" at the end, so `deviceclass.resource.kubernetes.io/<loser>` (which is unique and cannot collide) is never registered. The loser is then unreachable even by its own implicit name.

3. Deleting the loser removes the winner. `removeResourceName2class` deletes `resourceName2class[loser.ExtendedResourceName]` without checking that the entry belongs to the loser, so when a winner holds that explicit key, deleting the loser drops the winner's mapping.

4. Deleting the winner does not promote the runner-up. The cache only stores the current winner, not the candidate set, so once the winner is deleted nothing can restore the next class for that explicit name.

5. Renaming or updating the loser removes another class's mapping. The remove-old step deletes `resourceName2class[old.ExtendedResourceName]` unconditionally, so if the winner now owns that old key, updating the loser drops the winner's mapping.

The common root is that the cache keeps only the materialized winner per explicit name and mutates it in place, with no per-class ownership check and no record of the other candidates. The migration case the code intends to support (two DeviceClasses sharing an explicit `ExtendedResourceName`, newer wins) is exactly where these break.

I think the fix is to retain the candidate DeviceClasses per explicit name (or re-derive the winner from the full set on each event), keep implicit mappings independent of explicit-name arbitration, and remove a mapping only when it belongs to the class being changed. I am happy to send a fix and regression tests covering same-class update, loser add, loser delete, winner delete with runner-up promotion, winner and loser rename, and the equal-timestamp tie-break.

/kind bug
/sig scheduling
/wg device-management
/cc @yliaog

title: `StatefulSet` update stuck at the previous error
author: astraw99
body:
### What happened?

When update a `StatefulSet` image, if the pod get error like `ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff`, then if update the `StatefulSet` image again with a valid image, then the sts pod will stuck at the previous error, unless delete the error pod manually will trigger the new image rolling update.

Demo yaml to reproduce:
vim demo-sts.yaml
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: nginx-sts
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  serviceName: nginx
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.7.9
```
1). `kubectl apply -f demo-sts.yaml`, will see 3 pods running normally.
```
k get po
NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
nginx-sts-0   1/1     Running   0          10s
nginx-sts-1   1/1     Running   0          6s
nginx-sts-2   1/1     Running   0          5s
```
2). `kubectl edit sts nginx-sts` with a invalid image tag `nginx:1.7.9-a`, then will see:
```
k get po
NAME          READY   STATUS         RESTARTS   AGE
nginx-sts-0   1/1     Running        0          109s
nginx-sts-1   1/1     Running        0          105s
nginx-sts-2   0/1     ErrImagePull   0          4s
```
3). `kubectl edit sts nginx-sts` again with a valid image tag `nginx:1.8.1`, then will see the error pod will always stuck at the previous error, no rolling update.
```
k get po
NAME          READY   STATUS         RESTARTS   AGE
nginx-sts-0   1/1     Running        0          7m6s
nginx-sts-1   1/1     Running        0          7m2s
nginx-sts-2   0/1     ErrImagePull   0          3m12s
```
4). `k delete po nginx-sts-2` delete the error pod manually will trigger the new image rolling update to finish.
```

NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
nginx-sts-0   1/1     Running   0          8s
nginx-sts-1   1/1     Running   0          10s
nginx-sts-2   1/1     Running   0          17s
```

### What did you expect to happen?

`StatefulSet` update should not stuck at the previous error, shoud trigger rolling update with the latest update.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above.

Tested the issue on `Deployment/DaemonSet`, it is updated expectively.

title: kubectl rollout history: printer errors silently dropped when listing all revisions with -o flag
author: bhuvan-somisetty
body:
### What happened?

When running kubectl rollout history deployment/foo -o yaml (without --revision), errors returned by printer.PrintObj are silently discarded. The loop that iterates over all revisions calls printer.PrintObj(historyInfo[k], o.Out) without checking the error return value, so a broken pipe, a closed writer, or any other IO failure during output is invisible to the caller — the command exits 0 regardless.

**Relevant code:**
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/main/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/rollout/rollout_history.go#L195-L197

`go
for _, k := range sortedKeys {
    printer.PrintObj(historyInfo[k], o.Out)  // error return ignored
}
`

Compare with the single-revision path immediately above it (lines 186–188), which does handle the error correctly:

`go
if err := printer.PrintObj(revision, o.Out); err != nil {
    return err
}
`

### What did you expect to happen?

Any error from printer.PrintObj in the all-revisions loop should be returned and propagated, causing the command to exit non-zero, consistent with how every other code path in the same function behaves.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The easiest way to trigger this in a real cluster is to pipe the output to a program that exits early (causing a broken pipe):

`
kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp -o yaml | head -1
`

On Linux this will log a broken-pipe write error at the OS level, but kubectl will still exit 0 because the error from PrintObj is swallowed.

A unit test can inject a writer that returns an error to confirm the bug programmatically.

### Anything else we need to know?

The fix is straightforward: wrap the PrintObj call in the loop the same way the single-revision branch already does.

The existing test TestRolloutHistoryWithOutput in ollout_history_test.go covers the happy-path for yaml all revisions but has no case that injects a failing writer, so the bug is not caught by the test suite today. A test covering printer-error propagation should be added alongside the fix.

title: gofmt in go1.26.5 gives different output on amd64 and arm64, which breaks ci-kubernetes-verify-master-canary
author: dims
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

ci-kubernetes-verify-master-canary (the only verify job that runs on arm64 nodes, on the AKS build cluster)

### Which tests are failing?

verify-gofmt.sh

### Since when has it been failing?

First failure 2026-07-20 17:12 UTC, a few hours after #140000 merged. The job then alternated between green and red depending on which node it landed on. It has failed every run since 2026-07-29 17:06 UTC because every pod since then has landed on arm64 nodes.

### Testgrid link

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-k8s-infra-canaries#verify-master-canary

### Reason for failure (if possible)

gofmt from go1.26.5 does not produce the same output on amd64 and arm64 for one struct literal in `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/nodevolumelimits/csi.go` (added in #140000). The amd64 build of gofmt accepts the code as checked in. The arm64 build wants the short fields aligned to the long `enableInPlacePodVerticalScalingSchedulerPreemption` line. Each build rejects the form the other one wants, so running update-gofmt cannot produce a form both accept.

This is a bug in Go, not in the release binaries. The gofmt binaries in the CI image match the official go.dev tarballs, and building gofmt from unmodified go1.26.5 sources reproduces the difference purely by changing GOARCH. The cause is in go/printer, which decides where to break column alignment using a geometric mean computed with `math.Log` and `math.Exp` (nodes.go lines 232 to 287 in go1.26.5). Those functions can differ in the last bit between architectures, and the field lengths in this literal sit exactly on the 2.5 ratio threshold, so the decision flips. Presubmits run on amd64, which is why the change merged cleanly.

Evidence: the last green run (build 2082497666687700992, amd64 node) and the first red run of the streak (build 2082513014723973120, arm64 node) tested the same commit 7fbcad5e8ec.

### Anything else we need to know?

The fix on our side is to restructure the literal so the long field is assigned after the struct is built. I verified that form is accepted by gofmt from go1.26.5 on linux amd64, linux arm64, and darwin arm64, and by go1.27rc2. I will send a PR and file a golang/go issue for the printer bug.

title: Memory Manager pod-scope restore compares container blocks with the pod request
author: AutuSnow
body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager, after a kubelet restart, Memory Manager finds a restored container allocation and calls `regenerateHints` with that container's blocks and the whole Pod memory request.

For a multi-container Pod, those values differ, so `regenerateHints` returns no hint instead of restoring the Pod's previous NUMA hint. This can cause an existing Pod to fail admission under `restricted` or `single-numa-node`.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-scope hint restoration should use the restored pod-level allocation and preserve the previous NUMA hint.

### How can we reproduce it?

Use a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level memory resources and two containers, allocate it with static Memory Manager, restart from the checkpoint, then call `GetPodTopologyHints`. The current code returns no regenerated hint because it compares one container's blocks with the Pod request.

### Kubernetes version

`master` at `8e608f6b90e`

title: [Failing test] apisnoop-conformance-gate red since 2026-07-23: getLifecycleAPIGroup untested — pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml is not consumed by the gate
author: dims
labels: priority/important-soon, sig/node, kind/failing-test, sig/architecture, needs-triage, wg/node-lifecycle
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

- `apisnoop-conformance-gate` (periodic, every 3h)
- https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-arch-conformance#apisnoop-conformance-gate
- https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/apisnoop-conformance-gate

### Which tests are failing?

The gate itself:

```
==================
UNTESTED ENDPOINTS
getLifecycleAPIGroup

==================
ERROR: You have 1 untested endpoints
==================
```

### Since when has it been failing?

First red build: [2080099338675032064](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/apisnoop-conformance-gate/2080099338675032064) (2026-07-23 01:15 UTC).
Last green build: [2080053868456054784](https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/logs/apisnoop-conformance-gate/2080053868456054784) (2026-07-22 22:14 UTC).
Every run since has failed (~60 consecutive builds as of 2026-07-30), and `testgrid-num-failures-to-alert: '1'` means this alerts on every run.

### Reason for failure

#137050 (merged 2026-07-23 00:33 UTC, 42 minutes before the first red build) added the `lifecycle.k8s.io/v1alpha1` group (EvictionRequest). The group discovery path `/apis/lifecycle.k8s.io/` has no version in it, so its operation `getLifecycleAPIGroup` registers as **stable** in apisnoop even though the group only serves an alpha version. No conformance test can hit it (the group is not served in a default/conformance cluster), so the gate flags it as an untested eligible endpoint.

#137050 anticipated this and added `getLifecycleAPIGroup` to [`test/conformance/testdata/pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/conformance/testdata/pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml) — **but the `apisnoop-conformance-gate` job never reads that file**. The gate (snoopdb image) only loads `ineligible_endpoints.yaml`:

- [`303_fn_load_ineligible_endpoints.sql`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/initdb/303_fn_load_ineligible_endpoints.sql) fetches only `test/conformance/testdata/ineligible_endpoints.yaml`
- the untested list is `conformance.new_endpoint` = stable endpoints in the latest release minus `ineligible_endpoint` ([`207_view_conformance_new_endpoints.sql`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/initdb/207_view_conformance_new_endpoints.sql), [`203_view_conformance_eligible_endpoint.sql`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/initdb/203_view_conformance_eligible_endpoint.sql))
- [`docker-entrypoint.sh`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/snoopdb/postgres/docker-entrypoint.sh) exits 1 if that list is non-empty

`pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml` is only consumed by:
- test-infra's [`experiment/audit/audit_log_parser.py`](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/experiment/audit/audit_log_parser.py) (the `conformance-audit` jobs in `config/jobs/kubernetes/sig-arch/conformance-audit.yaml`)
- the apisnoop web UI ([`apps/web/src/lib/constants.js`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop/blob/main/apps/web/src/lib/constants.js))

### Anything else we need to know?

- #140923 was filed for this failure and closed as a duplicate of #140523, but #140523 tracks adding EvictionRequest CRUD tests — that cannot turn this gate green while the group is alpha-only (the endpoint is not served in a conformance cluster, and alpha APIs cannot have conformance tests). #140897 was closed unmerged. So nothing currently open unblocks the job.
- Precedent for exactly this situation is an entry in **`ineligible_endpoints.yaml`** (the file the gate does consume). `getInternalApiserverAPIGroup`, `getResourceAPIGroup`, and `getStoragemigrationAPIGroup` all have entries there with reason *"The endpoint is part of a group that has no stable endpoints yet, reporting as a stable endpoint in apisnoop."* (see also kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop#859, the identical failure for `storagemigration`).

Proposed fix:

1. **Short term (unblocks CI):** move `getLifecycleAPIGroup` from `pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml` to `ineligible_endpoints.yaml` with the same reason/link as the existing `get*APIGroup` entries, and remove it once `lifecycle.k8s.io` serves a stable version with conformance coverage (#140523).
2. **Longer term:** make snoopdb's gate also honor `pending_eligible_endpoints.yaml` (kubernetes-sigs/apisnoop), so the documented escape hatch actually applies to `apisnoop-conformance-gate`, or document that only `ineligible_endpoints.yaml` gates CI.

title: in-place resizing of Guaranteed pods breaks conformance tests if "static" CPU Manager policy is used
author: cbf123
body:
### What happened?

In Kubernetes v1.36.0, an restriction (introduced in PR#128287 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128287) blocks all in-place resource resizing of Guaranteed QoS pods on any node where the CPU Manager uses the static policy. The kubelet immediately rejects the resize with "Resize is infeasible for Guaranteed Pods alongside CPU Manager policy static".

### What did you expect to happen?

Given that the "static" CPU Manager policy is documented as an option, the testcase should simply be skipped if the node is using the "static" policy and does not have the InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs gate enabled.

At a high level I also think an argument could be made that https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128287/commits/2d8939c4aef8f060d413bb27272ba38cd7171fbe is too aggressive, and should allow resize of "guaranteed" pods on a node with a "static" CPU manager policy as long as the pod isn't using integer CPU requests (which result in exclusive CPU allocation).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Set the "static" CPU Manager policy on all nodes, then run the tests at https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.37.0-beta.0/test/conformance/testdata/conformance.yaml#L2601-L2629

### Anything else we need to know?

In Kubernetes v1.36.0, a restriction (introduced in PR#128287 - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128287) blocks all in-place resource resizing of Guaranteed QoS pods on any node where the CPU Manager uses the static policy. The kubelet immediately rejects the resize with "Resize is infeasible for Guaranteed Pods alongside CPU Manager policy static".

The Pod InPlace Resize Guaranteed pod multi-container conformance tests are new in the K8s v1.36 conformance suite.   The tests create Guaranteed pods with fractional milliCPU requests (25m, 17m, 29m) that run on the shared CPU pool, but the kubelet blanket-blocks resize for all Guaranteed pods on nodes with static CPU policy, causing the tests to time out after 300 seconds.

The StarlingX project (which we're running conformance on) enables the static CPU manager policy by default on all nodes, which causes it to always fail the new Guaranteed pod in-place resize testing in the conformance tests.

title: unit-master-dependencies: TestCelCostStability fails with cel-go v0.30.0 because runtime costs changed
author: dims
labels: sig/api-machinery, kind/failing-test, sig/architecture, area/dependency, area/code-organization, needs-triage, area/code-organization/future-dependencies
body:
### Which jobs are failing?

ci-kubernetes-unit-dependencies

https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-arch-code-organization#unit-master-dependencies

### Which tests are failing?

- TestCelCostStability/listMap_access/self.listMap.exists(m,_m.v2_==_'z') (runtime cost 22, expected 24)
- TestCelCostStability/listMap_access/!self.listMap.all(m,_m.v2_!=_'z') (runtime cost 20, expected 22)

Package: k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apiserver/schema/cel

### Since when has it been failing?

2026-07-26. The last green run started at 00:19 UTC and the first red run started at 04:19 UTC. Both runs tested the same kubernetes commit, so the cause is outside our repo.

### Reason for failure

The job updates every dependency to the latest release before running the unit tests. cel-go v0.30.0 was published at 03:54 UTC on 2026-07-26, inside that window.

In cel-go v0.30.0, cel-expr/cel-go#1369 changed `==`, `!=`, and strict binary calls so they stop before evaluating the right hand side when the left hand side is an error. The cost observer in cel-go only charges a call when it has seen all of the argument values, so these calls stopped being charged. Both failing expressions compare a field that is unset on two of the three list elements, so each one now reports a cost that is lower by 2.

Costs only went down. That is safe for existing CRDs because the compatibility rule only forbids cost increases. It still breaks these tests because they pin exact values.

### Anything else we need to know?

I proposed a fix upstream in cel-expr/cel-go#1394. It keeps the lazy evaluation from #1369 and only fixes the cost accounting. With that fix applied on top of v0.30.0, the full k8s schema/cel test package passes with no changes on our side.

There are two ways to make the job green:

1. Upstream accepts cel-expr/cel-go#1394 and cuts a patch release from the v0.30.0 base. We then bump to that release with no test changes.
2. We bump to cel-go v0.30.0 as it is and update the two pinned values. I have this ready as well.

One more warning. Testing our suite against current cel-go master (past v0.30.0) shows more cost changes coming in the next release: one optMap expression goes up from 8 to 9 at runtime, and four estimated costs go up as well (for example 22 to 31). Increases are the direction our compatibility rule forbids, so we should raise this upstream before v0.31.0 is cut.

title: [Feature][Scheduler] PodGroup/CompositePodGroup scheduling failure diagnosis is insufficient for debugging
author: KunWuLuan
body:
## PodGroup/CompositePodGroup scheduling failure diagnosis is insufficient for debugging

### Problem

When a PodGroup (gang) fails to schedule, the diagnostic information surfaced to users — via pod conditions, pod events, and PodGroup conditions — is incomplete, misleading, and does not scale to large gangs. CompositePodGroup failures are even worse: the root CPG gets no conditions at all, and propagated messages lose hierarchy context.

This was tested on a kind cluster built from `master` (v1.37.0-beta.0, commit `7c2b6c32644`) with `GenericWorkload`, `CompositePodGroup`, and `TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling` feature gates enabled.

### Related work

- #138991 proposes machine-readable scheduling diagnostics for individual Pods, but explicitly excludes Gang Scheduling / WAS-specific diagnostics ("avoid solving feature-specific diagnostics for Gang Scheduling, DRA, or preemption in the first step"). This issue focuses on the complementary problem: aggregated, human-readable diagnosis at the PodGroup and CompositePodGroup level, which is a WAS-specific concern that #138991 does not cover.
- PR #140311 (merged) propagated preemption status messages to PodGroup conditions. This issue extends that idea to all scheduling failure modes, not just preemption.
- KEP-6012 (CompositePodGroup API) defines the `CompositePodGroupInitiallyScheduled` condition type in the API, but the scheduler never patches it — no writer exists. This issue tracks that gap.

### Current behavior — observed from testing

#### Scenario 1: PodGroup with gang scheduling (minCount=2, 2 pods requesting 100 cpu)

| Object | Condition | Message |
|---|---|---|
| `gang-pod-1` | `PodScheduled=False` | `0/2 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s).` |
| `gang-pod-2` | `PodScheduled=False` | `pod group is unschedulable, 0/1 placements are available, first placement status: minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining` |
| PodGroup `gang-fail` | `PodGroupInitiallyScheduled=False` | `...minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining, pod group preemption: No preemption victims found for incoming preemptor` |

**Issues:**
- `gang-pod-1` (evaluated first) retains its per-node `FitError`. `gang-pod-2` (evaluated second, after `PlacementFeasible` returned `Unschedulable`) gets a generic group-level message with no per-node diagnosis.
- In a gang with 100 pods, only the first-evaluated pod gets a useful `FitError`. The other 99 pods all get the same generic message. Users cannot tell which pods failed or why.
- The PodGroup condition does not aggregate per-pod failure reasons.

#### Scenario 2: CompositePodGroup (minGroupCount=2, 2 child PodGroups, each with 1 pod requesting 100 cpu)

| Object | Condition | Message |
|---|---|---|
| `cpg-pod-1` | `PodScheduled=False` | `0/2 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s).` |
| `cpg-pod-2` | `PodScheduled=False` | `pod group is unschedulable, 0/1 placements are available, first placement status: minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining` |
| PodGroup `child-pg-1` | `PodGroupInitiallyScheduled=False` | `...minCount (1) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 0 remaining...` |
| PodGroup `child-pg-2` | `PodGroupInitiallyScheduled=False` | `...minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining...` |
| CompositePodGroup `cpg-root` | **(none)** | **No conditions patched at all** |

**Issues:**
- `child-pg-2` has `minCount: 1` in its spec, but its condition says `minCount (2)`. The "2" is actually the CPG root's `minGroupCount`, propagated verbatim by `completeCompositePodGroupAlgorithmResultMap` (`schedule_one_podgroup.go`). The "scheduled/remaining" counts refer to child **groups**, not pods — but the message doesn't say that.
- `cpg-root` has no conditions. The `CompositePodGroupInitiallyScheduled` condition type is defined in the API (`staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1alpha3/types.go:1387`) but never written — `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` explicitly skips CompositePodGroups.
- Neither pod's message mentions the CPG hierarchy. A user seeing `minCount (2) cannot be satisfied` on `cpg-pod-2` has no way to know this came from `cpg-root` without manually walking `spec.parentCompositePodGroupName` references.

### Root causes in code

1. **Individual pod `FitError` is destroyed by group-level propagation.** In `completeCompositePodGroupAlgorithmResultMap` (`schedule_one_podgroup.go:755`), when a parent CPG fails, the child's entire `podGroupAlgorithmResult` (including per-pod `podResults`) is replaced with the parent's status. Individual `FitError`s are lost.

2. **`PlacementFeasible` message is ambiguous.** `GangScheduling.PlacementFeasible` (`gangscheduling.go`) uses the same message format for both PodGroup (`MinCount` = pod count) and CompositePodGroup (`MinGroupCount` = child group count): `"minCount (%d) cannot be satisfied: %d scheduled, %d remaining"`. No group name, no indication of what "scheduled/remaining" counts.

3. **No diagnosis aggregation at the PodGroup level.** `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` sets the PodGroup condition message to `podGroupResult.status.Message()` — the raw group-level status. The per-pod `algorithmResult` data (which nodes each pod was placed on, which nodes rejected it, and why) is available at this point but discarded.

4. **CompositePodGroup conditions are never patched.** `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult` skips CPGs (`if pgi.CompositePodGroup != nil { continue }`). No `PatchCompositePodGroupStatus` utility exists.

### Proposal

Design a layered diagnosis mechanism: Pod → PodGroup → CompositePodGroup, where each layer provides the right granularity and cross-references the others.

#### 1. Pod level: preserve individual diagnosis, add group context

In `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult`, stop overwriting individual pod statuses with generic group messages:

- **Pod individually failed**: keep its `FitError` as-is (already works for the first-evaluated pod).
- **Pod individually succeeded but group failed**: `"pod is schedulable but gang scheduling failed (PodGroup <name>): <group reason>. See PodGroup condition for details."`
- **Pod never evaluated** (gang aborted early): `"pod was not evaluated: gang scheduling aborted early (PodGroup <name>). See PodGroup condition for failure summary."`

This ensures every pod's condition tells the user whether the failure is pod-level or group-level, and where to find details.

#### 2. PodGroup level: aggregated placement narrative + failure signatures

Build a structured diagnosis message from `podGroupAlgorithmResult.podResults`, which contains per-pod `SuggestedHost` (placement node) and `FitError.Diagnosis.NodeToStatus` (structured per-node rejection reasons).

**Small gang (≤10 pods)** — list each pod:

```
Gang scheduling failed: 2/5 pods placed, minCount=4.

Placement:
  node-A: pod-1 (cpu:4, mem:1Gi), pod-2 (cpu:4, mem:1Gi)

Failed pods:
  pod-3: node-A: Insufficient cpu; node-B: untolerated taint
  pod-4: node-A: Insufficient cpu; node-B: untolerated taint
  pod-5: not evaluated (gang aborted)
```

This shows the causal relationship: pod-1 and pod-2 consumed 8 cpu on node-A, so pod-3/pod-4 got `Insufficient cpu` on node-A.

**Large gang (>10 pods)** — aggregate by node and by failure signature:

```
Gang scheduling failed: 30/100 pods placed, minCount=80.

Placement by node (30 pods):
  node-A: 15 pods (cpu: 60/64)
  node-B: 10 pods (cpu: 40/64)
  node-C: 5 pods (cpu: 20/64)

Failed pods (70), by failure signature:
  45 pods: Insufficient cpu
  15 pods: Insufficient cpu + untolerated taint
  10 pods: Insufficient memory

Top rejecting nodes:
  node-A: rejected 70/70 failed pods (Insufficient cpu — 60/64 cpu used by placed pods)
  node-B: rejected 50/70 failed pods (Insufficient cpu — 40/64 cpu used by placed pods)
```

Key design decisions:
- **Failure signature grouping**: extract the set of unique rejection reasons from each pod's `FitError.Diagnosis.NodeToStatus`, group pods with identical reason sets. This preserves the combination relationship (e.g., "Insufficient cpu + untolerated taint" is distinct from "Insufficient cpu") while compressing 100 pods into a few lines.
- **Placement by node with resource usage**: aggregate placed pods per node, showing total requested resources vs. node allocatable. This lets users see why subsequent pods were rejected on that node.
- **Top rejecting nodes**: cross-reference placement and rejection — "node-A rejected 70 pods for Insufficient cpu, and node-A has 60/64 cpu used by placed pods." The causal link is explicit.

#### 3. CompositePodGroup level: patch conditions + hierarchy context

- Implement `PatchCompositePodGroupStatus` (analogous to existing `PatchPodGroupStatus` in `pkg/scheduler/util/utils.go`).
- In `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult`, stop skipping CPGs — patch `CompositePodGroupInitiallyScheduled` condition.
- In `completeCompositePodGroupAlgorithmResultMap`, annotate propagated messages with the source CPG name: `"failed via CompositePodGroup <name>: <reason>"`.
- In `PlacementFeasible`, distinguish pods vs. child groups in the message: `"CompositePodGroup <name>: minGroupCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining child groups"`.

CPG condition format:

```
CompositePodGroupInitiallyScheduled=False

Composite gang scheduling failed: 0/2 child groups schedulable, minGroupCount=2.
  child-pg-1: 0/1 pods placed (minCount=1). Failure: Insufficient cpu.
  child-pg-2: 0/1 pods placed (minCount=1). Failure: Insufficient cpu.
```

#### 4. `PlacementFeasible` message improvement

Current:
```
minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining
```

Proposed (PodGroup):
```
PodGroup gang-fail: minCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining pods
```

Proposed (CompositePodGroup):
```
CompositePodGroup cpg-root: minGroupCount (2) cannot be satisfied: 0 scheduled, 1 remaining child groups
```

### Scope

- All changes are in scheduler internals (`schedule_one_podgroup.go`, `gangscheduling.go`, `util/utils.go`).
- No API type changes — all information fits in existing `metav1.Condition.Message` fields.
- No changes to the scheduling algorithm itself — only to how results are reported.

### Files involved

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go` | `submitPodGroupAlgorithmResult`: build aggregated diagnosis, patch CPG conditions |
| `pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go` | `completeCompositePodGroupAlgorithmResultMap`: annotate propagated messages with CPG name |
| `pkg/scheduler/schedule_one_podgroup.go` | New: `buildPodGroupDiagnosis`, `aggregateFailureSignatures`, `buildPlacementMap` |
| `pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/gangscheduling/gangscheduling.go` | `PlacementFeasible`: include group name, distinguish pods vs. child groups |
| `pkg/scheduler/util/utils.go` | New: `PatchCompositePodGroupStatus` |

title: High volume of Pod lifecycle events during scale tests causes API Server throttling (APF rejections) and etcd bloat
author: aojea
body:
@michaelasp and I were during high-churn scale testing using Clusterloader2 (creating and deleting approximately 50,000 pods in a 5-minute window), and we observed a massive volume of event generation that severely impacted the API control plane. 

We analyzed a sample of 145,259 events generated during a 5-minute window and found that **91% of them were generated by the Kubelet** (`Killing`, `Started`, `Created`, `Pulled` events), and **9% by the Scheduler** (`Scheduled` events).

For every pod lifecycle transition, Kubelet writes multiple events. At scale, this results in an event storm. 

We traced the event generation to the following locations in the Kubernetes codebase:

*   **`Killing` events** (34.08% of total events): Generated when containers are stopped.
    *   **Code Reference:** [`pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go) in `killContainer()`:
        ```go
        if len(message) == 0 {
            message = fmt.Sprintf("Stopping container %s", containerSpec.Name)
        }
        m.recordContainerEvent(ctx, pod, containerSpec, containerID.ID, v1.EventTypeNormal, events.KillingContainer, "%v", message)
        ```
*   **`Created` and `Started` events** (~38% combined): Generated during container startup.
    *   **Code Reference:** [`pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_container.go) in `startContainer()`:
        ```go
        m.recordContainerEvent(ctx, pod, container, containerID, v1.EventTypeNormal, events.CreatedContainer, "Container created")
        ...
        m.recordContainerEvent(ctx, pod, container, containerID, v1.EventTypeNormal, events.StartedContainer, "Container started")
        ```
*   **`Pulled` events** (18.83%): Generated by the image manager.
    *   **Code Reference:** [`pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go):
        ```go
        m.logIt(logger, objRef, v1.EventTypeNormal, events.PulledImage, logPrefix, fmt.Sprintf("Successfully pulled image %q...", ...))
        ```

The volume of these event writes had severe consequences on the control plane and they seem to be used just for informational purposes:

1.  **API Priority and Fairness (APF) Throttling:**
    The API Server queue limits were exceeded, leading to the rejection of critical control plane requests:
    *   **`system-nodes` (Kubelet traffic):** **5,069 requests rejected** due to `queue-full`. Kubelets were throttled when communicating with the API server.
    *   **`kube-scheduler`:** **3,710 requests rejected** due to `queue-full`, directly delaying scheduling.
    *   **`kube-system-service-accounts`:** **2,365 requests rejected** due to `queue-full`.
2.  **etcd Database Bloat:**
    The etcd database size reached **2.89 GB** (`apiserver_storage_size_bytes`) due to the high volume of writes (nearly 2.9 million etcd write operations for events recorded by etcd metrics). This size persists even after namespace deletion until manual defragmentation is run, risking etcd quota exhaustion.
3.  **Increased Latency:**
    The average API server latency for event creation (`POST`) rose to **113.82 ms**, with a significant tail of requests taking up to **8 seconds**.

These facts can be validated by querying the API server `/metrics` endpoint during or immediately after a high-churn test:

```prometheus
apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total{flow_schema="system-nodes",reason="queue-full"}
apiserver_flowcontrol_rejected_requests_total{flow_schema="kube-scheduler",reason="queue-full"}
```

```prometheus
apiserver_storage_size_bytes{storage_cluster_id="etcd-0"}
```

```prometheus
apiserver_request_duration_seconds_bucket{resource="events",verb="POST"}
etcd_request_duration_seconds_bucket{resource="events",operation="create"}
```


Should the Kubelet event rate-limiting defaults be more aggressive during high pod churn, or should certain verbose events (like `Pulled` for already present images) be demoted or omitted?

title: High cardinality on apiserver_request_terminations_total metric
author: jpbetz
body:
The apiserver_request_terminations_total metric (alpha stability level) has unbounded cardinality due to labels build from unvalidated request paths:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7ed622c80f39f99dc9efc8275fd1244b1791fa67/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/metrics/metrics.go#L195-L202

The `RequestInfo` used to populate the group, version, resource, and subresource labels is parsed directly from the raw request path segments and is not validated.

To bound this metric we should drop the unvalidated labels and only keep `verb`, `scope`, component` and `code`.

title: CPU Manager AllocatePod re-allocates restored pod CPUs after kubelet restart
author: AutuSnow
body:
### What happened?

With pod-scope Topology Manager and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, static CPU Manager is not idempotent across kubelet restart.

After restart, pod-level CPU assignments are restored from the checkpoint. Existing Pods then go through admission again, and Topology Manager calls `AllocatePod(AddOperation)`. In `allocatePodForAdd`, the pod-scope path does not check whether a complete pod-level allocation was already restored. It allocates again from the default CPU set and overwrites the restored pod assignment.

This causes two deterministic failure modes:

- If the remaining default CPU set cannot satisfy the same request again, kubelet rejects an existing Pod after restart.
- If enough CPUs remain, CPU Manager assigns a second CPU set and overwrites the restored pod assignment, while the original CPUs stay removed from the default set, effectively leaking exclusive CPUs.

Examples with 1 reserved CPU and a Pod requesting 2 CPUs:

```text
4 CPUs:
restored pod cpuset:     1-2
restored default cpuset: 0,3
readmission error:       not enough cpus available to satisfy request: requested=2, available=1

6 CPUs:
pod cpuset:              1-2 -> 3-4
default cpuset:          0,3-5 -> 0,5
readmission error:       <nil>
```

The current path is here: [`allocatePodForAdd`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5f91251764f106ba06c25a612d646ff612392e35/pkg/kubelet/cm/cpumanager/policy_static.go#L397-L440). It calls `allocateCPUs` and `SetPodCPUSet` without consulting the restored pod allocation.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod-level CPU Manager allocation should be idempotent across kubelet restart.

If a complete pod-level allocation was restored from checkpoint, post-restart admission should preserve the restored pod CPU set, container assignments, and default CPU set. It should not allocate a second CPU set or reject the existing Pod because of its own restored reservation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A deterministic unit test can extend `TestCPUManagerRestoreState`:

1. Enable `PodLevelResources` and `PodLevelResourceManagers`.
2. Configure static CPU Manager with pod-scope Topology Manager, 1 reserved CPU, and either 4 or 6 single-threaded CPUs.
3. Create a Guaranteed Pod with pod-level request/limit of 2 CPUs and 1 container.
4. Start CPU Manager and call `AllocatePod` once.
5. Add the container so the pod/container assignments are checkpointed.
6. Recreate CPU Manager with the same checkpoint dir to simulate kubelet restart.
7. Verify the pod CPU set, container assignment, and default CPU set were restored.
8. Call `AllocatePod(AddOperation)` again.
9. Verify the restored state is unchanged.

Observed results:

- On 4 CPUs: `not enough cpus available to satisfy request: requested=2, available=1`
- On 6 CPUs: the restored pod CPU set changes from `1-2` to `3-4`, and the default CPU set changes from `0,3-5` to `0,5`

### Anything else we need to know?

This is the CPU Manager counterpart of #140906.

This is separate from #129078 / #129079. Those concern the older container-level `full-pcpus-only` SMT validation path. This reproducer does not enable `full-pcpus-only`; it exercises the pod-level allocation path introduced by #134768.

`PodLevelResourceManagers` was promoted to Beta and enabled by default for Kubernetes 1.37 in #140573.

### Kubernetes version

`master` commit `5f91251764f106ba06c25a612d646ff612392e35`

title: DaemonSet pod can be permanently stuck Pending when its target node is saturated by equal-priority pods during mass rescheduling
author: yogeshbendre
body:
### What happened?

**TL;DR:** DaemonSet pods get no priority advantage over regular pods. Since a DaemonSet pod can only ever run on the one specific node it targets, if that node fills up with equal-priority pods first, the DaemonSet pod is stuck `Pending` forever — preemption only evicts strictly *lower*-priority pods, so there is no recovery path. Reproducible deterministically in under a minute on vanilla Kubernetes (see "How can we reproduce it" below); also confirmed live on a real-world cluster after 11 days stuck with no self-healing.

After a batch of nodes were recreated (health-check driven remediation) and rejoined the cluster, a DaemonSet pod whose only eligible node (per its DaemonSet-generated node affinity) had already been filled to that node's pod capacity by pods belonging to an unrelated ReplicaSet remained `Pending` indefinitely — until an operator manually deleted another pod on that node to free capacity.

Sequence observed:

1. A node-health event caused several worker and control-plane nodes to be remediated (deleted and recreated) at roughly the same time, on a cluster topology of 3 control-plane + 5 worker nodes.
2. Pods that were running on the deleted worker nodes (from a 300-replica ReplicaSet with no `topologySpreadConstraints`) became unschedulable and queued up as Pending.
3. As replacement nodes rejoined the cluster one at a time, the scheduler bound the queued ReplicaSet pods to the first available node until it hit the kubelet's max-pods ceiling (110), before moving on to spread remaining pods across the other newly-available nodes.
4. The DaemonSet controller's pod for that same node could only ever target that one node (DaemonSet pods are scheduled via a node-specific affinity/nodeName, not floated across the cluster), but by the time it was considered, the node had no remaining pod capacity.
5. The DaemonSet pod and the ReplicaSet pods all ran at the same (default, unset) priority, so the DaemonSet pod could not trigger preemption to reclaim a slot on its required node.
6. Result: the DaemonSet pod stayed `Pending` indefinitely — not delayed, but permanently stuck, with no self-healing path — because there is no capacity-reservation or priority mechanism ensuring a DaemonSet pod can still land on its node once that node fills up with regular pods.

**Scheduler event observed on the stuck pod:**

```
Warning  FailedScheduling  (repeating)  default-scheduler
0/8 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods, 7 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity].
no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/8 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found
for incoming pod, 7 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.
```

**Only available workaround:** manually cordon the saturated node and delete one non-DaemonSet pod on it. The evicted pod reschedules elsewhere (node is cordoned); the DaemonSet pod then binds to the freed slot because DaemonSet pods tolerate `NoSchedule`. This requires manual identification of the affected node/pod per stuck DaemonSet and causes disruption to an unrelated, already-running workload — it is not a fix, and does not scale when multiple DaemonSets or many single-replica workloads are involved.


### What did you expect to happen?

A DaemonSet is a workload primitive with an implicit scheduling guarantee: exactly one pod per eligible node. That guarantee should not be silently defeated by unrelated workloads racing to fill node capacity during bulk/concurrent node-Ready events. Expected behavior is one of:

- The scheduler/kubelet admission path reserves headroom for DaemonSet pods on a node before admitting other pending pods, similar in spirit to how DaemonSet pods already bypass normal scheduling predicates for taints/tolerations; or
- DaemonSet pods are assigned a priority (or an equivalent mechanism) sufficient to preempt same/lower-priority pods on their required node when no other placement option exists for them, so they are not permanently blocked by a race they cannot participate in; or
- At minimum, this failure mode is called out as a documented limitation with a supported mitigation, rather than silently producing an unrecoverable Pending DaemonSet pod.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The original observation involved a large multi-node cluster and a mass node-remediation event, but neither is actually required to trigger the bug — that context is just *one* way a node ends up saturated by equal-priority pods. The minimal reproduction below removes all of that and triggers the same failure deterministically, in under a minute, on a 3-node [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/) (Kubernetes-in-Docker) cluster running vanilla, publicly-released upstream Kubernetes. No cloud provider, no CNI plugin choice, no node churn simulation needed.

**Prerequisites:** Docker and `kind` installed locally.

```bash
# 1. Create a 3-node cluster (1 control-plane + 2 workers)
cat > kind-config.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
- role: control-plane
- role: worker
- role: worker
EOF
kind create cluster --name daemonset-repro --config kind-config.yaml

# 2. Cap one worker's pod capacity low, so saturating it is cheap (real default is 110; using
#    8 here just makes the repro fast — the mechanism is identical at 110)
docker exec daemonset-repro-worker sh -c "echo 'maxPods: 8' >> /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml"
docker exec daemonset-repro-worker systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro get node daemonset-repro-worker \
  -o jsonpath='capacity.pods={.status.capacity.pods}{"\n"}'
# -> capacity.pods=8   (2 of those 8 are already taken by kube-proxy + the CNI daemonset pod)

# 3. Saturate that worker with a plain Deployment: default priority, no
#    topologySpreadConstraints, pinned to the capped node via nodeSelector so it's deterministic
#    which node fills up
cat > filler-deploy.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: filler
spec:
  replicas: 8
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: filler}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: filler}
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/hostname: daemonset-repro-worker
      tolerations:
      - operator: Exists
      containers:
      - name: pause
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
EOF
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro apply -f filler-deploy.yaml
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro describe node daemonset-repro-worker | grep "Non-terminated Pods"
# -> Non-terminated Pods:          (8 in total)      <- node is now completely full

# 4. Deploy a real DaemonSet across the cluster (no priorityClassName — same as any
#    unmodified example DaemonSet manifest)
cat > ds.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: nginx-daemonset
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: nginx-daemonset}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: nginx-daemonset}
    spec:
      tolerations:
      - operator: Exists
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10
EOF
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro apply -f ds.yaml
kubectl --context kind-daemonset-repro get pods -o wide -l app=nginx-daemonset
```

**Actual output, captured just now:**

```
NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   NODE
nginx-daemonset-6w8q2   1/1     Running   0          10s   daemonset-repro-worker2
nginx-daemonset-hqq47   0/1     Pending   0          10s   <none>
nginx-daemonset-j7ggb   1/1     Running   0          10s   daemonset-repro-control-plane
```

The pod for the saturated worker is immediately and permanently `Pending`:

```
$ kubectl describe pod nginx-daemonset-hqq47
...
Priority:         0
...
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  21s   default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods,
  2 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity]. no new claims to deallocate, preemption:
  0/3 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod, 2 Preemption is not
  helpful for scheduling.

$ kubectl get pod nginx-daemonset-hqq47 -o jsonpath='{.spec.affinity.nodeAffinity}'
{"requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution":{"nodeSelectorTerms":[{"matchFields":
[{"key":"metadata.name","operator":"In","values":["daemonset-repro-worker"]}]}]}}

$ kubectl get pod nginx-daemonset-hqq47 filler-7d95777f96-6rxvg \
    -o jsonpath='{.spec.priority}{"\n"}{.spec.priority}{"\n"}'
0
0
```

Identical signature to the original report: node-pinned `NodeAffinity` on `metadata.name`, both pods at priority `0`, and `No preemption victims found for incoming pod`. This state does not resolve on its own — polling the pod hours later shows the same event repeating, exactly as in the 11-day-stuck pods described further below.

Kubernetes version for this run: `kindest/node:v1.36.1` (vanilla, publicly released upstream build — this repro has no dependency on any downstream distribution or unreleased version).

#### Is this ordering-dependent, or does it reproduce under a fair, simultaneous race?

The steps above deliberately create the blocking pods before the DaemonSet pod, which trivially guarantees a loss. To check whether the failure is an artifact of that ordering, we re-ran it two more ways on the same live cluster, deleting an already-`Running`, steady-state DaemonSet pod and an already-`Running` set of filler pods together, then letting both controllers race to recreate replacements for the freed capacity — the actual dynamic during a real node recovery, where nothing is deliberately sequenced.

- **Fully simultaneous deletion, no pre-existing backlog advantage:** both the DaemonSet pod and 5 filler pods on a node were force-deleted in the same command. The DaemonSet's replacement pod *won* one of the 6 freed slots and stayed `Running`. This is an honest, useful negative result: a genuinely concurrent race between freshly-created pods is probabilistic, not a guaranteed DaemonSet loss — the scheduler has no bias against DaemonSet pods specifically when everything enters the queue at the same moment.
- **Freed single slot with a pre-existing backlog (matches the original incident's actual mechanics):** with 15 filler-pod replicas already sitting `Pending` beforehand — a long-queued backlog, exactly like the 300-replica overflow in the original report — we deleted only the running DaemonSet pod, freeing exactly one slot. A backlog pod created **26 seconds before** the DaemonSet's replacement pod even existed claimed the slot instantly. The DaemonSet's new replacement was left with the identical `FailedScheduling` / `No preemption victims found for incoming pod` signature, confirmed still `Pending` 30+ seconds later.

This second variant is the faithful reproduction of the real-world trigger, and it isn't a coin flip: a DaemonSet controller can only create its replacement pod *after* it observes the old one is gone, which is necessarily later than pods that were already queued and waiting for capacity before the node came back. Against an already-waiting backlog, the DaemonSet pod is structurally late to the scheduling queue every time, not merely unlucky — which is exactly the sequence described in the original incident ("as soon as the first worker node comes back, scheduler tries to assign all the pending pods to that node... the daemonset pod remains in pending state"). The first variant shows the underlying preemption gap has no protective bias either way when pods start even; the second shows why, in the specific conditions that actually occur during a mass-remediation event, the DaemonSet pod reliably loses.


### Anything else we need to know?

### Where this happens in the code

Traced against the `v1.35.0` tag and confirmed live on `v1.36.1` (see the reproduction above). Four pieces combine to produce this failure mode; none of them is broken in isolation — each does exactly what it's documented to do — but the composition leaves DaemonSet pods with no recovery path once their one eligible node saturates.

**1. A DaemonSet pod is hard-pinned to exactly one node, with no fallback**

`pkg/controller/daemon/util/daemonset_util.go`, `ReplaceDaemonSetPodNodeNameNodeAffinity` ([L176-221](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/controller/daemon/util/daemonset_util.go#L176-L221)) rewrites the pod's `NodeAffinity` into a `RequiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` match on `metadata.name` for one specific node before the pod is created. Once that pod exists, it has exactly one place in the entire cluster it can ever bind to — if that node can't admit it, it is `Pending` with no alternative, by design.

**2. The DaemonSet controller never assigns the pod an elevated priority**

`pkg/controller/daemon/daemon_controller.go` (1472 lines in this tag) has zero references to `Priority`/`PriorityClassName` anywhere in the file — the controller copies the user's pod template verbatim and leaves priority entirely up to whatever (if anything) the DaemonSet author put in `spec.template.spec.priorityClassName`. Nothing defaults it, validates it, or nudges toward it. Contrast this with core system DaemonSets like `kube-proxy`, which only avoid this failure mode by convention — their manifests explicitly set `priorityClassName: system-node-critical`. That convention is not enforced anywhere in the DaemonSet API or controller, so any user-authored DaemonSet (including the minimal nginx one used in the repro above, and most example manifests in the docs) ships without it.

**3. With no PriorityClassName set, admission assigns priority 0 — identical to any other pod**

`plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go`, `admitPod` ([L162-172](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L162-L172)): on create, if `pod.Spec.PriorityClassName` is empty, the plugin calls `getDefaultPriority()` and stamps the result onto the pod. That resolves to `scheduling.DefaultPriorityWhenNoDefaultClassExists`, defined in `pkg/apis/scheduling/types.go` ([L24-28](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/apis/scheduling/types.go#L24-L28)) as literal `0` — unless the cluster happens to have a PriorityClass with `globalDefault: true`. A vanilla ReplicaSet pod with no priority class gets exactly the same value. By the time both pods reach the scheduler, there is nothing distinguishing the DaemonSet pod from the ReplicaSet pod.

**4. The preemption path categorically excludes equal-priority pods as victims**

`pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/defaultpreemption/default_preemption.go`, `isPreemptionAllowed` ([L349-352](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.35.0/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/defaultpreemption/default_preemption.go#L349-L352)):

```go
func (pl *DefaultPreemption) isPreemptionAllowed(nodeInfo fwk.NodeInfo, victim fwk.PodInfo, preemptor *v1.Pod) bool {
	// The victim must have lower priority than the preemptor, in addition to any filtering implemented by IsEligiblePod
	return corev1helpers.PodPriority(victim.GetPod()) < corev1helpers.PodPriority(preemptor) && pl.IsEligiblePod(nodeInfo, victim, preemptor)
}
```

This is a strict `<`, not `<=`. Given step 3, both the DaemonSet pod and the ReplicaSet pods on the saturated node carry priority `0`, so this check evaluates `false` for every pod on that node. The scheduler reports `preemption: ... No preemption victims found for incoming pod` — exactly the event captured in this report — and there is no retry path, because nothing about the node's occupancy changes on its own once the ReplicaSet pods are `Running`.

**Putting it together:** (1) removes every fallback placement option for the DaemonSet pod. (2)-(4) remove the only mechanism — preemption — that could reclaim space once the node fills. Each function is working as documented; the gap is structural: a DaemonSet pod using a template without an explicit, elevated `priorityClassName` has no guaranteed recovery path once its one eligible node saturates with equal-or-higher-priority pods. This is why we believe the most direct fix point is (2)/(3) — either give DaemonSet pods an elevated default priority (mirroring the `system-node-critical` convention used by core system DaemonSets) so they can preempt when they have no alternative node, or add a DaemonSet-aware carve-out in `IsEligiblePod`/`isPreemptionAllowed` for a pod's uniquely-eligible node — rather than at (1) or the general scheduling-imbalance behavior tracked in #136782, since fixing spread alone would reduce how often the node saturates but would not remove the permanent-stuck outcome once it does.

### Live evidence (second, independent cluster)

In addition to the vanilla kind reproduction above, this was also confirmed on a second, independent real-world cluster — a downstream Kubernetes distribution (3 control-plane + 5 worker RHEL nodes, Antrea CNI; the original incident was observed on both Antrea and Calico clusters, so it isn't CNI-specific;) — separate from the cluster where this was first observed. Two DaemonSet pods were found stuck `Pending` for 11 days at the time of capture:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Stuck pod priority | `nginx-daemonset-2c96z` and `nginx-daemonset-nsb7r`: both `Priority: 0`, no `priorityClassName` |
| FailedScheduling event | `0/8 nodes are available: 1 Too many pods, 7 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity]. no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/8 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod, 7 Preemption is not helpful for scheduling.` — repeated **3186 times over 11 days** for each pod. It never self-heals. |
| Node pin (matches code path 1) | Each pod's `nodeAffinity` is a `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` match on `metadata.name` for exactly one node — e.g. `{"matchFields":[{"key":"metadata.name","operator":"In","values":["<single-node>"]}]}`. No alternative placement exists. |
| DaemonSet template priority (matches code path 2/3) | `kubectl get ds nginx-daemonset -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.priorityClassName}'` → empty. No elevated priority requested anywhere. |
| Target node saturation | Both target nodes: `capacity.pods=110`, `allocatable.pods=110`, `describe node` confirms `Non-terminated Pods: (110 in total)` — exactly at the ceiling, not over/under. |
| Blocking pods' priority (matches code path 4) | Sampled `nginx-rs-new` replica pods occupying both saturated nodes: `priority=0` on every one checked, and the ReplicaSet template has no `priorityClassName` and no `topologySpreadConstraints`. Identical priority to the stuck DaemonSet pod → `isPreemptionAllowed`'s strict `<` check excludes them all as victims, exactly as traced in the code above. |

Two independently-stuck pods on a cluster unrelated to the one where this was first reported rules out a one-off fluke and confirms every link in the "Where this happens in the code" chain against a live, current build.

### Other notes

- This was first noticed as an apparent regression after node remediations triggered by an unrelated control-plane availability issue, but the scheduling behavior itself is version/platform-agnostic once the preconditions above are met — it is a race between DaemonSet placement and bulk regular-pod placement, not specific to any particular trigger for node churn.
- Related to [#136782](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/136782), which describes the scheduler concentrating a burst of newly-schedulable pods onto the first available node rather than spreading them during a scale-up event. That issue is about scheduling *imbalance*; this issue is about the *lack of any recovery path* once a DaemonSet's sole eligible node is filled by equal-priority pods — a fix to the spreading behavior in #136782 would reduce how often this triggers, but would not eliminate it, since any single saturating event is sufficient to strand a DaemonSet pod indefinitely.
- Also related: [#54190](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/54190) ("DaemonSet controller should support preemption"), filed in 2017, which proposed essentially the same fix point identified independently here (point 2/3 above). It appears to have gone unimplemented — this report includes a concrete, current-version reproduction and code trace in case that's useful context for re-opening the discussion.
- Workaround guidance we are currently giving is to set [topologySpreadConstraints](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints/) on all production workloads to reduce the odds of a single node saturating. This is a mitigation on the "other" workloads, not a fix, and it is not something the platform can enforce or guarantee for arbitrary workloads, so DaemonSets remain structurally exposed to this failure mode.


### Kubernetes version

<details>
Minimal reproduction (above): `kindest/node:v1.36.1`, vanilla upstream, via kind — publicly reproducible with no dependency on any particular distribution.

Also independently observed on a downstream Kubernetes distribution in real-world use (see "Live evidence" above.
